# Ubuntu 24.04 Playground

Welcome to your isolated **Ubuntu 24.04** container environment running as a Kubernetes pod.

## Prerequisites & Tools
This container comes pre-configured with:
- `bash`
- `curl`, `wget`, `git`
- `iproute2` (`ip a`, `ip route`), `net-tools`
- `procps` (`ps aux`, `top`)
- `vim`, `nano`

---

## Guided Exercises

### Step 1: Inspect System Release & Kernel
Run the following command in the interactive terminal on the right to view your OS version:

```bash
cat /etc/os-release
uname -a
```

### Step 2: Working Directory & Environment Variables
Check your current working directory and active shell environment:

```bash
pwd
whoami
env | grep USER
```

### Step 3: Create a DevOps Workspace Directory
Create a directory named `devops` in your home directory:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/devops && cd ~/devops
pwd
```

---

## Tasks Checklist

tasks.title: Check Ubuntu OS Version
tasks.description: Execute `cat /etc/os-release` in the terminal to verify the container image.

tasks.title: Create ~/devops Directory
tasks.description: Create a directory named `devops` inside your home directory.

tasks.title: Create hello.txt file
tasks.description: Write "Welcome to BYOLabs" into a file named `hello.txt` inside ~/devops.
tasks.validationScript: grep -i "Welcome to BYOLabs" ~/devops/hello.txt || grep -i "Welcome to BYOLabs" /root/devops/hello.txt

labs.instructionsMarkdown:
# Podman Playground (Standard GKE Cluster)

Welcome to your isolated **Podman Playground** running with full rootful container capabilities on the **Standard Kubernetes Cluster**!

---

## What is Podman?
**Podman** (Pod Manager) is an open-source, daemonless, OCI-compliant container engine developed by Red Hat. Unlike Docker, Podman:
- Operates **without a background daemon** (`dockerd`) — every container is a direct child of the Podman process (managed via Conmon).
- Provides native support for **Pods** (groups of containers sharing network and namespaces, identical to Kubernetes Pods).
- Can generate and play Kubernetes YAML manifests directly using `podman kube generate` and `podman kube play`.
- CLI syntax is 1:1 compatible with Docker (`alias docker=podman`).

---

## Guided Exercises

### Step 1: Inspect Podman Engine & Host Environment
Verify your Podman version and check the underlying OCI runtime (`crun`), storage graph driver (`overlay`), and network backend (`netavark`):

```bash
podman --version
podman info
```

### Step 2: Pull and Manage OCI Images
Pull a lightweight Alpine Linux image from Docker Hub or Fedora registry:

```bash
podman pull alpine
podman images
```

### Step 3: Run Interactive and Background Containers
Run a container using Podman:

```bash
# Run a one-off Alpine container
podman run --rm alpine uname -a

# Run a named container in background
podman run --name my-alpine -d alpine sleep 3600
podman ps -a
```

### Step 4: Work with Podman Pods
Podman's flagship feature is managing pods without requiring a Kubernetes cluster:

```bash
# Create a new Pod named web-pod
podman pod create --name web-pod -p 8080:80

# List pods
podman pod ps

# Run a container inside the pod
podman run -d --pod web-pod --name web-server nginx:alpine
podman pod inspect web-pod
```

---

## Tasks Checklist

tasks.title: 1. Verify Podman Engine & Version
tasks.description: Run `podman --version` or `podman info` in the terminal to inspect the active Podman engine.

tasks.title: 2. Pull Alpine Container Image
tasks.description: Pull the `alpine` image from registry using `podman pull alpine`.
tasks.validationScript: podman images | grep -q "alpine" || podman image exists alpine

tasks.title: 3. Run a Container with Podman
tasks.description: Run a container named `my-alpine` or any container using `podman run`.

tasks.title: 4. Create a Podman Pod
tasks.description: Create a Podman pod named `web-pod` using `podman pod create --name web-pod`.
tasks.validationScript: podman pod exists web-pod || podman pod ps | grep -q "web-pod"

labs.instructionsMarkdown:
# Kubernetes Pods & Workload Basics (KinD Cluster)

Welcome to your isolated, dedicated **Kubernetes v1.31** cluster powered by KinD (Kubernetes in Docker)!
You have full **`cluster-admin`** privileges inside this environment.

---

## ⚡ Verification & Getting Started
Your cluster bootstraps automatically on startup (~18s). Check your single-node control plane:

```bash
kubectl get nodes
kubectl cluster-info
alias k=kubectl
```

---

## Guided Exercises

### Step 1: Create a Custom Namespace
Isolate application workloads inside a dedicated namespace:

```bash
kubectl create namespace dev
kubectl get namespaces
```

### Step 2: Deploy an Imperative Pod
Launch a standalone Nginx pod inside the `dev` namespace:

```bash
kubectl run web-pod --image=nginx:alpine -n dev
kubectl get pods -n dev
```

### Step 3: Create a Scalable Deployment
Deploy a replicated web application:

```bash
kubectl create deployment api-server --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2 -n dev
kubectl get deployments -n dev
kubectl get pods -n dev -l app=api-server
```

### Step 4: Expose the Deployment with a Service
Create a Service to balance traffic across the pods:

```bash
kubectl expose deployment api-server --port=80 --type=NodePort -n dev
kubectl get svc -n dev
```

### Step 5: Declarative YAML Manifest
Practice writing and applying a declarative YAML manifest:

```bash
cat << 'EOF' > my-app.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: demo-app
  namespace: dev
  labels:
    tier: frontend
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
EOF

kubectl apply -f my-app.yaml
kubectl get pod demo-app -n dev
```

labs.name: Containerd & ctr Image Lifecycle Playground
labs.description: Hands-on Containerd runtime playground. Master the industry-standard CNCF container runtime using ctr: image distribution, namespaces, container tasks, and runtime lifecycle debugging.
labs.instructionsMarkdown:
# Containerd & ctr Lifecycle Playground

Welcome to your isolated **Containerd** container environment running on the Kubernetes cluster.

---

## What is Containerd?
**Containerd** is an industry-standard, core container runtime developed as a CNCF graduated project. It powers modern Docker and manages the complete container lifecycle of Kubernetes worker nodes (via CRI).

### Core Concepts:
- **Daemon**: `containerd` daemon running as a background service listening on `/run/containerd/containerd.sock`.
- **Namespaces**: Containerd isolates images and containers within distinct namespaces (e.g. `default`, `k8s.io`, `moby`).
- **Containers vs Tasks**: In Containerd, a *Container* holds the metadata, configuration, and image spec. A *Task* represents the actual running process executing on the host.

---

## Guided Exercises

### Step 1: Verify Containerd Runtime & Version
Inspect the active Containerd daemon and CLI client:

```bash
ctr version
ctr check
```

### Step 2: Manage Containerd Namespaces
Containerd uses namespaces to prevent naming collisions between subsystems:

```bash
# List all active namespaces
ctr namespaces list
# (or shorthand: ctr ns ls)

# Create a custom namespace for your project
ctr namespaces create devops
ctr ns ls
```

### Step 3: Pull & Inspect OCI Images
Pull an official image from Docker Hub into Containerd:
*(Note: ctr requires fully-qualified registry references, e.g. docker.io/library/<image>:<tag>)*

```bash
# Pull Alpine Linux into default namespace
ctr images pull docker.io/library/alpine:latest

# List pulled images
ctr images list
# (or shorthand: ctr i ls)
```

### Step 4: Run Containers & Manage Tasks
Launch and monitor a container task:

```bash
# 1. Run an interactive one-off command
ctr run --rm -t docker.io/library/alpine:latest test-box uname -a

# 2. Run a detached background task
ctr run -d docker.io/library/alpine:latest alpine-worker sleep 3600

# 3. List active containers and running tasks
ctr containers list
ctr tasks list
```

### Step 5: Stop & Remove Tasks and Containers
Stop the process and clean up the container:

```bash
# Stop/kill running task
ctr tasks kill -s SIGKILL alpine-worker

# Delete task and container definition
ctr tasks rm alpine-worker
ctr containers rm alpine-worker
```

---

## Tasks Checklist

tasks.title: 1. Verify Containerd Runtime (ctr version)
tasks.description: Run `ctr version` in your terminal to verify client and daemon connectivity.

tasks.title: 2. Create a Containerd Namespace ("devops")
tasks.description: Create a new Containerd namespace named `devops` using `ctr namespaces create devops` (or `ctr ns create devops`).
tasks.validationScript: ctr namespaces list | grep -q "devops" || ctr ns ls | grep -q "devops"

tasks.title: 3. Pull Alpine Image with ctr
tasks.description: Pull the official Alpine image using `ctr images pull docker.io/library/alpine:latest`.
tasks.validationScript: ctr images list | grep -q "alpine" || ctr -n devops images list | grep -q "alpine"

tasks.title: 4. Run an Alpine Container Task (alpine-worker)

tasks.validationScript: ctr containers list | grep -q "alpine-worker" || ctr tasks list | grep -q "alpine-worker" || ctr -n devops containers list | grep -q "alpine-worker"

labs.name: Buildah OCI Image Builder Playground
labs.description: Daemonless container image creation with Buildah. Build OCI images step-by-step from base images or scratch, manipulate container root filesystems directly, and compile Dockerfiles without running a Docker daemon.
labs.instructionsMarkdown:
# Buildah OCI Image Builder Playground

Welcome to your isolated **Buildah Playground**! Practice daemonless, secure OCI container builds without needing a running Docker daemon.

---

## What is Buildah?
**Buildah** is a command-line tool developed by Red Hat and the open-source containers community. Unlike Docker:
- **No background daemon** (`dockerd`) is required.
- Builds can be performed inside unprivileged containers or rootless CI/CD pipelines.
- Supports **interactive builds**: construct container images command-by-command directly from the shell or scripting.
- Allows direct host filesystem mounts of container root filesystems (`buildah mount`).
- Fully compatible with Dockerfiles via `buildah bud` (Build Using Dockerfile).

---

## Guided Exercises

### Step 1: Inspect Buildah Engine & Configuration
Verify your Buildah version and check storage configuration:

```bash
buildah --version
buildah info
```

### Step 2: Interactive Container Construction
Buildah lets you start a container from a base image and build up layers interactively:

```bash
# 1. Create a working container from Alpine
container=$(buildah from alpine)
echo "Working container created: $container"

# 2. Run commands inside the build container
buildah run $container sh -c 'echo "Created with Buildah on BYOLabs" > /etc/byolabs.txt'
buildah run $container cat /etc/byolabs.txt

# 3. Configure container metadata, entrypoint, or environment variables
buildah config --author "DevOps Engineer" $container
buildah config --env APP_ENV=production $container
buildah config --entrypoint '["cat", "/etc/byolabs.txt"]' $container

# 4. Commit the container to a new OCI image
buildah commit $container my-custom-image:v1

# 5. Clean up the working container
buildah rm $container
```

### Step 3: Declarative Image Builds with Dockerfile (buildah bud)
You can also build images using standard Dockerfiles using `buildah bud`:

```bash
# Create a sample Dockerfile
mkdir -p ~/myapp && cd ~/myapp
cat << 'EOF' > Dockerfile
FROM alpine:latest
RUN echo "Hello from Buildah Dockerfile" > /hello.txt
CMD ["cat", "/hello.txt"]
EOF

# Build image tagged webapp:latest
buildah bud -t webapp:latest .

# Verify the newly built image
buildah images
```

### Step 4: Direct Filesystem Mounts (buildah mount)
One of Buildah's most powerful features is modifying container filesystems directly on the host without starting a container process:

```bash
new_box=$(buildah from alpine)
mountpoint=$(buildah mount $new_box)
echo "Mounted at: $mountpoint"

# Write directly to container filesystem via host path
echo "Direct disk injection" > "$mountpoint/direct.txt"
cat "$mountpoint/direct.txt"

# Unmount when done
buildah unmount $new_box
buildah rm $new_box
```

---

## Tasks Checklist

tasks.description: Run `buildah --version` or `buildah info` in the terminal to inspect the Buildah runtime.

tasks.title: 2. Create a Working Container from Alpine
tasks.description: Create a new working container using `buildah from alpine`.

tasks.title: 3. Commit Custom Image (my-custom-image:v1)
tasks.description: Commit your working container into a new image named `my-custom-image:v1` using `buildah commit <container> my-custom-image:v1`.

tasks.title: 4. Build Image using Dockerfile (buildah bud -t webapp:latest .)
tasks.description: Create a Dockerfile and compile it into an image tagged `webapp:latest` using `buildah bud -t webapp:latest .`.

labs.name: Terraform Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Fundamentals
labs.description: Master declarative Infrastructure as Code using HashiCorp Terraform. Practice HCL syntax, provider declarations, resource dependencies, local state management, execution plans, and input/output variables.
labs.instructionsMarkdown:
# Terraform Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Fundamentals

Welcome to your dedicated **HashiCorp Terraform** sandbox environment running in an isolated container.

---

## 🛠️ What is Terraform?
**Terraform** is the industry standard for declarative **Infrastructure as Code (IaC)**. With Terraform, you describe your desired infrastructure topology in human-readable HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL). Terraform then generates an execution plan and provisions the infrastructure safely and deterministically.

### The Core Terraform Workflow:
1. **Write**: Define resources and providers in `.tf` configuration files.
2. **Init** (`terraform init`): Initialize the working directory and install required provider plugins.
3. **Plan** (`terraform plan`): Preview changes that Terraform will make against the active state.
4. **Apply** (`terraform apply`): Provision or mutate the declared resources.
5. **Destroy** (`terraform destroy`): Tear down managed infrastructure.

---

## 🚀 Guided Exercises

### Step 1: Verify the Terraform CLI
Check your installed Terraform version in the interactive terminal:

```sh
terraform version
terraform -help
```

### Step 2: Create a Working Directory & Provider Spec
Create a dedicated workspace directory `/root/terraform-lab` and declare a `local` provider in `main.tf`:

```sh
mkdir -p /root/terraform-lab && cd /root/terraform-lab

cat << 'EOF' > main.tf
terraform {
  required_providers {
    local = {
      source  = "hashicorp/local"
      version = "~> 2.5.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "local" {}

resource "local_file" "config" {
  content  = "environment = production\napp_name = byolabs-api\nmanaged_by = terraform\n"
  filename = "${path.module}/app-config.conf"
  file_permission = "0644"
}

resource "local_file" "inventory" {
  content  = "[webservers]\n10.0.1.10\n10.0.1.11\n"
  filename = "${path.module}/hosts.ini"
}
EOF
```

### Step 3: Initialize the Project (`terraform init`)
Download and initialize the local provider plugin:

```sh
terraform init
ls -la .terraform
```

### Step 4: Plan & Apply Infrastructure (`terraform apply`)
Generate the execution plan and apply the declared configuration:

```sh
terraform plan
terraform apply -auto-approve

# Inspect the generated configuration files
ls -la
cat app-config.conf
cat hosts.ini
```

### Step 5: Declare Outputs and Variables
Add input variables and output expressions:

```sh
cat << 'EOF' > outputs.tf
output "config_file_path" {
  description = "Path to generated config file"
  value       = local_file.config.filename
}

output "config_file_id" {
  description = "SHA1 ID of the config file"
  value       = local_file.config.id
}
EOF

terraform apply -auto-approve
terraform output
```

### Step 6: Inspect Active State
Verify state management commands:

```sh
terraform show
terraform state list
```

---

## 📋 Tasks Checklist

labs.name: Ansible Automation & Playbook Fundamentals
labs.description: Master agentless IT automation with Ansible. Practice creating inventory hosts, executing ad-hoc commands, authoring YAML playbooks, managing file resources, and ensuring idempotent execution.
labs.instructionsMarkdown:
# Ansible Automation & Playbook Fundamentals

Welcome to your dedicated **Ansible Control Node** environment running in an isolated container.

---

## 🛠️ What is Ansible?
**Ansible** is an open-source, agentless IT automation engine. It automates cloud provisioning, configuration management, application deployment, and intraservice orchestration using simple, human-readable YAML playbooks.

### Core Architecture Concepts:
- **Control Node**: The machine where Ansible is installed and from which automation is run.
- **Inventory**: A list of managed nodes (hosts) organized into groups (INI or YAML format).
- **Modules**: Discrete units of code executed by Ansible (e.g. `ping`, `command`, `copy`, `file`).
- **Playbooks**: YAML specifications declaring the desired end-state across managed hosts.
- **Idempotency**: Running a playbook multiple times produces the same result without unintended changes.

---

## 🚀 Guided Exercises

### Step 1: Verify Ansible Control Node
Check your installed Ansible engine and Python environment:

```sh
ansible --version
ansible-config dump --only-changed
```

### Step 2: Set Up Workspace & Local Inventory
Create your project folder `/root/ansible-lab` and declare a local target in `inventory.ini`:

```sh
mkdir -p /root/ansible-lab && cd /root/ansible-lab

cat << 'EOF' > inventory.ini
[local]
localhost ansible_connection=local ansible_python_interpreter=/usr/bin/python3

[webservers]
web-01 ansible_connection=local
EOF
```

### Step 3: Run Ad-Hoc Commands
Execute immediate ad-hoc modules without writing a playbook:

```sh
# Test connectivity using the ping module
ansible localhost -i inventory.ini -m ping

# Run a shell command via command module
ansible localhost -i inventory.ini -m command -a "df -h"

# Collect system facts
ansible localhost -i inventory.ini -m setup -a "filter=ansible_distribution*"
```

### Step 4: Author a Multi-Task Playbook
Create a complete automation playbook `site.yml`:

```sh
cat << 'EOF' > site.yml
---
- name: Enterprise System Setup Playbook
  hosts: localhost
  connection: local
  gather_facts: false
  vars:
    app_name: "byolabs-worker"
    target_dir: "/tmp/byolabs"

  tasks:
    - name: Ensure target directory exists
      ansible.builtin.file:
        path: "{{ target_dir }}"
        state: directory
        mode: '0755'

    - name: Deploy application release metadata
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        dest: "{{ target_dir }}/release.json"
        content: |
          {
            "app": "{{ app_name }}",
            "version": "1.0.0",
            "status": "ready"
          }
        mode: '0644'

    - name: Generate verification stamp
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        dest: "/tmp/ansible-verified.txt"
        content: "Ansible Playbook completed successfully on BYOLabs!\n"
        mode: '0644'
EOF
```

### Step 5: Syntax Check & Run the Playbook
Verify YAML syntax and execute the playbook:

```sh
ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml --syntax-check
ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml

# Inspect the generated artifacts
cat /tmp/byolabs/release.json
cat /tmp/ansible-verified.txt
```

### Step 6: Test Playbook Idempotency
Run the playbook a second time. Notice that tasks report `ok` instead of `changed`:

```sh
ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml
```

---

## 📋 Tasks Checklist

tasks.title: 1. Verify Ansible Installation (ansible --version)
tasks.description: Execute `ansible --version` in the terminal to inspect the active Ansible installation.

tasks.title: 2. Configure Inventory with Local Target
tasks.description: Create `/root/ansible-lab/inventory.ini` containing `localhost` configured with `ansible_connection=local`.

tasks.title: 3. Execute Successful Ad-hoc Ping

tasks.validationScript: ansible localhost -i /root/ansible-lab/inventory.ini -m ping 2>/dev/null | grep -q "SUCCESS" || ansible localhost -i ~/ansible-lab/inventory.ini -m ping 2>/dev/null | grep -q "SUCCESS" || ansible localhost -m ping 2>/dev/null | grep -q "SUCCESS"

tasks.title: 4. Execute Playbook and Generate Artifacts
tasks.description: Run `site.yml` using `ansible-playbook` to generate `/tmp/ansible-verified.txt` and `/tmp/byolabs/release.json`.

labs.name: openSUSE Leap Administration & Zypper Playground
labs.description: Hands-on openSUSE Leap enterprise sandbox. Master the Zypper package manager (zypper refresh, install, search), RPM repository administration, user management, and openSUSE system administration.
labs.instructionsMarkdown:
# openSUSE Leap Administration & Zypper Playground

Welcome to your isolated **openSUSE Leap** container environment running as a Kubernetes pod.

---

## 🦎 What is openSUSE Leap?
**openSUSE Leap** is a community Linux distribution that shares its core codebase with **SUSE Linux Enterprise (SLE)**. It is known for its rock-solid stability, enterprise-grade package management, and system administration tooling.

### The Zypper Package Manager:
`zypper` is the powerful command-line interface for the `libzypp` package management library. Common commands include:
- `zypper lr`: List configured repositories.
- `zypper ref`: Refresh metadata from remote repositories.
- `zypper in <pkg>`: Install a package.
- `zypper rm <pkg>`: Remove a package.
- `zypper se <pkg>`: Search for available packages.
- `zypper info <pkg>`: View detailed package metadata.

---

## 🚀 Guided Exercises

### Step 1: Inspect openSUSE System Information
Verify your OS release and kernel details in the interactive terminal:

```bash
cat /etc/os-release
cat /etc/SUSE-brand
uname -a
```

### Step 2: Query Zypper Repositories
Inspect the active openSUSE repositories:

```bash
# List repositories with detailed URLs and aliases
zypper lr -d

# Refresh repository metadata caches
zypper refresh
```

### Step 3: Search and Query Packages
Search the repositories for system tools:

```bash
zypper search --details curl
zypper info vim
```

### Step 4: Install System Utilities with Zypper
Install packages non-interactively:

```bash
zypper --non-interactive install -y tree vim

# Verify installed binaries
which tree
tree --version
```

### Step 5: System Administration & User Provisioning
Create a new administrative user following openSUSE defaults:

```bash
useradd -m -s /bin/bash -c "SUSE Systems Admin" suseadmin
id suseadmin
ls -la /home/suseadmin
```

### Step 6: Query RPM Database Directly
Inspect installed packages using the low-level RPM command:

```bash
rpm -qa | grep -i opensuse
rpm -qil tree
```

---

## 📋 Tasks Checklist

tasks.title: 1. Inspect openSUSE OS Release
tasks.description: Execute `cat /etc/os-release` in the terminal to inspect the openSUSE distribution.

tasks.title: 2. Query Active Zypper Repositories
tasks.description: Run `zypper lr` in the terminal to inspect active package repositories.

tasks.title: 3. Install "tree" via Zypper
tasks.description: Install the `tree` utility using `zypper --non-interactive install -y tree`.

tasks.title: 4. Create Administrative User "suseadmin"
tasks.description: Create user `suseadmin` with a home directory and bash shell using `useradd -m -s /bin/bash suseadmin`.

labs.name: Git Branching, Merge Conflicts & Interactive Rebase
labs.description: Master real-world Git version control workflows. Practice feature branching, simulating and resolving three-way merge conflicts, rebasing feature commits onto main, and inspecting DAG commit history.
labs.instructionsMarkdown:
# Git Branching, Merge Conflicts & Interactive Rebase

Welcome to your dedicated **Git Advanced Workflows** container environment.

---

## 🛠️ What You Will Master
In enterprise DevOps and software engineering, engineers collaborate across multiple feature branches. Merges don't always apply cleanly, and linear Git histories require mastering rebasing. This lab guides you through:
1. Branch creation and HEAD pointers.
2. Generating divergent commits across parallel branches.
3. Understanding Git merge conflict markers (`<<<<<<< HEAD`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`).
4. Manually resolving conflicts and recording clean merge commits.
5. Rebasing feature branches onto `main` for a clean, linear commit graph.

---

## 🚀 Guided Exercises

### Step 1: Configure Git Identity & Initialize Workspace
Set up global identity and create the workspace directory `/root/git-advanced`:

```bash
git config --global user.name "DevOps Engineer"
git config --global user.email "engineer@byolabs.in"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

mkdir -p /root/git-advanced && cd /root/git-advanced
git init
```

### Step 2: Create Main Branch with Initial Codebase
Create `app.py` and commit it to the `main` branch:

```bash
cat << 'EOF' > app.py
# BYOLabs Web Application Core
VERSION = "1.0.0"

def get_status():
    return {"status": "ok", "service": "api-gateway"}

def handle_request():
    print("Processing request standard pipeline")
EOF

git add app.py
git commit -m "feat: initial commit with api-gateway core"
git branch -M main
```

### Step 3: Create Feature Branch "feature/auth"
Branch off `main` and make modifications to `app.py`:

```bash
git checkout -b feature/auth

cat << 'EOF' > app.py
# BYOLabs Web Application Core
VERSION = "1.1.0-auth"

def get_status():
    return {"status": "ok", "service": "api-gateway", "auth": "jwt"}

def handle_request():
    print("Processing request with OAuth2 JWT validator")
EOF

git commit -am "feat(auth): integrate JWT token validation pipeline"
```

### Step 4: Create Divergent Commit on Main Branch
Switch back to `main` and make a conflicting edit to `app.py`:

```bash
git checkout main

cat << 'EOF' > app.py
# BYOLabs Web Application Core
VERSION = "1.1.0-metrics"

def get_status():
    return {"status": "ok", "service": "api-gateway", "telemetry": "prometheus"}

def handle_request():
    print("Processing request with OpenTelemetry metrics")
EOF

git commit -am "feat(telemetry): add Prometheus metrics collector"
```

### Step 5: Merge and Resolve Conflict
Trigger a merge conflict and resolve it cleanly:

```bash
# Trigger the merge conflict
git merge feature/auth || true

# Inspect the conflict markers
cat app.py

# Resolve the conflict by combining both features
cat << 'EOF' > app.py
# BYOLabs Web Application Core
VERSION = "1.1.0"

def get_status():
    return {"status": "ok", "service": "api-gateway", "auth": "jwt", "telemetry": "prometheus"}

def handle_request():
    print("Processing request with OAuth2 JWT validator and OpenTelemetry metrics")
EOF

git add app.py
git commit -m "merge: resolve conflict combining auth and telemetry"
```

### Step 6: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main
Create a second feature branch and rebase it linearly onto updated `main`:

```bash
git checkout -b feature/cache
echo '# Redis cache client' > cache.py
git add cache.py
git commit -m "feat(cache): add redis caching interface"

# Rebase cleanly onto main
git rebase main

# Inspect the commit DAG graph
git log --graph --oneline --decorate --all
```

---

## 📋 Tasks Checklist

tasks.title: 1. Initialize /root/git-advanced & Configure Identity
tasks.description: Initialize git in `/root/git-advanced` and configure `user.name` and `user.email`.

tasks.title: 2. Create Base Commit on "main" Branch
tasks.description: Create `app.py` and commit it to the `main` branch with `git commit`.

tasks.title: 3. Create "feature/auth" Branch with Custom Commit
tasks.description: Create and checkout branch `feature/auth`, modify `app.py`, and commit changes.

tasks.title: 4. Merge "feature/auth" into "main" & Resolve Conflicts
tasks.description: Merge `feature/auth` into `main`, resolve conflict markers in `app.py`, and complete the merge commit.

tasks.title: 5. Create & Rebase "feature/cache" onto "main"
tasks.description: Create branch `feature/cache` with `cache.py`, and rebase it onto `main` with `git rebase main`.
tasks.validationScript: git -C /root/git-advanced rev-parse --verify feature/cache >/dev/null 2>&1 && [ "$(git -C /root/git-advanced merge-base main feature/cache)" = "$(git -C /root/git-advanced rev-parse main)" ]
